draft.title: Buddhist bioethics
card: Bioethics asks what is right in medicine and at the beginning and end of life. Buddhists have no single ruling on these issues. Teachers and traditions draw on shared ideas and reach different views.
Precept
The first precept is to refrain from harming or taking life. It is a training rule that many Buddhists apply to abortion and euthanasia, since both can involve ending a life.
Compassion
Compassion (karuna) is concern to relieve suffering. Some Buddhists argue it supports easing the pain of a dying person. Others say it does not allow ending a life.
Intention

Intention (cetana) matters in judging an act, because kamma is shaped by the thought behind it. Acts done with care and without hatred or greed are weighed differently from acts done with those motives.
draft.remember: Buddhists weigh the first precept, compassion and intention together, and may reach different views.

a.q: Why do Buddhists not all agree about euthanasia?
opts: They weigh the precept, compassion and intention differently
They accept the first precept only for monks and nuns
They hold that compassion has no place in medical choices
They hold that intention has no effect on the weight of an act
a.why: Buddhists share the same ideas but apply them in different ways, so views differ. It is wrong to say they reject compassion or intention, as the card shows both are used in judging an act.
a.clue: Think about how the same three ideas can be applied.

b.q: Kenji, a Buddhist, says a doctor's act should be judged partly by the doctor's state of mind, not only by its result. Which idea is he using?
opts: Intention, since kamma is shaped by the thought behind an act
The first precept, since it bans every medical act
Compassion, since it judges every act by its result
Bioethics, since it gives one ruling for all Buddhists
b.why: Kenji is pointing to intention, which shapes kamma and so the weight of an act. The precept is tempting, but it is about not harming life and does not by itself say that state of mind matters.
b.clue: Which idea is about the thought behind an act?

proposal.title: Buddhist bioethics
card: Bioethics asks what is right in medicine and at the beginning and end of life. Buddhists have no single ruling on these issues. Teachers and traditions draw on shared ideas and reach different views.
Precept

The first precept is to refrain from harming or taking life. It is a training rule that many Buddhists apply to euthanasia and to the loss of spare embryos in IVF, since both can involve ending a life.
Compassion

Compassion (karuna) is concern to relieve suffering. Some Buddhists argue it supports easing the pain of a dying person, or helping a couple have a child through IVF. Others say it does not allow ending a life.
Intention

Intention (cetana) matters in judging an act, because kamma is shaped by the motive behind it. Acts done with care and without hatred or greed are weighed differently from acts done with those motives.
proposal.remember: Buddhists weigh the first precept, compassion and intention together, and may reach different views.

a.q: Why do Buddhists not all agree about euthanasia?
opts: They weigh the precept, compassion and intention differently
They accept the first precept only for monks and nuns
They hold that compassion has no place in medical choices
They hold that intention plays no part in judging an act
a.why: Buddhists share the same ideas but apply them in different ways, so views differ. It is wrong to say they reject compassion or intention, as the card shows both are used in judging an act.
a.clue: Think about how the same three ideas can be applied.

b.q: Kenji, a Buddhist, says a doctor's act should be judged partly by the doctor's state of mind, not only by its result. Which idea is he using?
opts: Intention, as it shapes the kamma that follows an act
The first precept, as it judges an act by its motive
Compassion, as it judges an act by how it turns out
Bioethics, as it is the study of a doctor's moods
b.why: Kenji is pointing to intention, which shapes kamma and so the weight of an act. The first precept is tempting, but it is a rule about not harming or taking life, not a way of weighing motives.
b.clue: Kenji cares about why the doctor acted, not just what happened.
